newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Klaus vows to fight on, govt still seen weak.
newsitem.headline: Klaus vows to fight on, govt still seen weak.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, under fire over his handling of the economy, vowed on Friday to fight on for the ruling coalition's economic programme but analysts said his government still looked weak.
Faced with calls for his resignation and a possible no-confidence vote in his unpopular government, Klaus promised to fight for his political life on the floor of parliament.

"I am resolutely repeating that I am ready to take on the political fight over these steps on the floor of parliament and that I am not ready to run away from the fight," Klaus told a hastily-arranged news conference, shown live on television.

The Czech crown has for two weeks been under intense pressure as investors, alarmed at widening trade and current account deficits and mounting political uncertainty, sold the currency. The central bank eventually gave in to the pressure and floated the crown from Tuesday.

It fell again on Friday morning after opposition leader Milos Zeman of the Social Democrats said he would seek a parliamentary vote of no coinfidence in the centre-right coalition, but rebounded after Klaus's statement.
"It is a short-term positive that Klaus is not resigning but the medium-term problems are still there," said Matt Starr, head of capital markets at Creditanstalt in Prague.

Klaus's coalition, which holds 100 seats in the 200-seat lower house, on Wednesday unveiled an austerity package, including spending cuts and a public sector wage freeze, aimed at reviving the economy. However, with its popularity at record lows, analysts said he would struggle to implement it.

"It is possible that he will be able to hold things together but it is going to take an extraordinarily effective political process and, more importantly, a convincing policy," said Stephen Heintz of Prague's Institute of East-West Studies.
"I do not think he has the confidence of the people at large, which then translates into a real loss of confidence in parliament," he added.

Zeman said he would seek to have a motion of no confidence in the government moved in the lower house session beginning on July 1, saying the austerity package diverged sharply from the government's declared programme.
"What more mistakes must this government make for it to leave voluntarily," parliament chairman Zeman told reporters.

Klaus on Wednesday also announced a sweeping reshuffle of his cabinet, naming new finance, industry, trade and interior ministers. Interior Minister-designate Petr Necas has since withdrawn his candidacy and Jan Ruml has resumed his post.
Ivan Pilip, part of Klaus's inner circle, was named to replace Ivan Kocarnik as finance minister, whom many Czechs blamed for the economic problems.

"It is the old team with some new faces, but it is still the old team and for this old team to sell the new ideas to the public, it's a question of credibility," said Jiri Pehe, director of the regional specialists unit at Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.
Klaus, in power since the Czech Republic was established in 1993, is personally identified with its transition from a centrally-planned to a market economy.
"Klaus is very positive for the market. He always has been. It would be a great level of uncertainty if and when Klaus ever leaves," said Starr.
However, Pehe believed Klaus should go.
"Klaus has done some good things for this country, but he cannot see that his time has past. He is becoming counter-productive by staying in this position," he said.
